# Portfolio Analysis {#sec-bem-portfolio-analysis}

In Chapter 5, @bali2016 use portfolio sorts to study how next year's excess return varies with beta, market capitalization, and book-to-market.
We form portfolios at each December year-end from 1988 to 2012 using the panel from @sec-summary-statistics.
Holding returns run from 1989 to 2012.

{{< include _show-table.qmd >}}

```{python}
import polars as pl

from eap_pl import build_annual_panel

annual_panel = build_annual_panel()
```

```{python}
#| include: false

import io
import re
from pathlib import Path

from eap_pl import format_fit, hac


def read_annual_factors(path, columns):
    rows = re.findall(r"^\s*([0-9]{4},[^\n]+)", Path(path).read_text(), flags=re.MULTILINE)
    return pl.read_csv(
        io.StringIO("\n".join(row.replace(" ", "") for row in rows)),
        has_header=False,
        new_columns=columns,
        schema_overrides={"Holding year": pl.Int32},
    )


ff3 = read_annual_factors("data/ff3-201607.csv", ["Holding year", "MKT", "SMB", "HML", "RF"])
momentum = read_annual_factors("data/momentum-202412.csv", ["Holding year", "MOM"])
factors = ff3.drop("RF").join(momentum, on="Holding year", validate="1:1")

factor_models = {
    "Excess return": [],
    "CAPM": ["MKT"],
    "FF": ["MKT", "SMB", "HML"],
    "FFC": ["MKT", "SMB", "HML", "MOM"],
}
variable_labels = {"Beta": "Beta", "MktCap": "Market cap", "BM": "Book-to-market"}


def fit_portfolios(returns, columns, model="Excess return"):
    terms = factor_models[model]
    sample = returns.sort("year")
    if terms:
        sample = (
            sample.with_columns((pl.col("year") + 1).alias("Holding year"))
            .join(factors.select("Holding year", *terms), on="Holding year",
                  how="left", validate="1:1", maintain_order="left")
        )
    rhs = " + ".join(terms) or "1"
    return {
        column: hac(f"outcome ~ {rhs}", sample.select(pl.col(column).alias("outcome"), *terms))
        for column in columns
    }


def show_holding_year(returns):
    show_table(
        returns.select(pl.col("year").alias("Formation year"),
                       (pl.col("year") + 1).alias("Holding year"), pl.exclude("year"))
    )


def target_label(variable, group):
    return f"{variable_labels[variable]} " + {5: "4–1", 6: "average"}.get(group, str(group))


def show_grid(cells, control, target, *, holding=False):
    control_label = variable_labels[control]
    headings = {column: f"{control_label} {column}" for column in control_ports}
    headings.update({"Diff": f"{control_label} 3–1", "Avg": f"{control_label} average"})
    table = cells.with_columns(
        pl.col("target").replace_strict(
            {group: target_label(target, group) for group in range(1, 7)}
        )
    ).rename({"target": "Portfolio", **{c: h for c, h in headings.items() if c in cells.columns}})
    if holding:
        show_holding_year(table)
    else:
        show_table(table.rename({"year": "Year"}) if "year" in table.columns else table)


def grid_fits(returns):
    columns = [*control_ports, "Diff", "Avg"]
    return {
        (group, model): fit_portfolios(returns.filter(pl.col("target") == group), columns, model)
        for group in sorted(returns["target"].unique())
        for model in ["Excess return", "FFC"]
    }


def show_grid_fits(fits, *, dependent=False):
    columns = [*control_ports, "Avg"] if dependent else [*control_ports, "Diff", "Avg"]
    headers = [f"Beta {column}" for column in columns]
    rows = [
        [target_label("MktCap", group), label,
         *[format_fit(fits[group, model][column], "Intercept") for column in columns]]
        for group in range(1, 6 if dependent else 7)
        for model, label in [("Excess return", "Excess return"), ("FFC", "FFC alpha")]
    ]
    show_table(pl.DataFrame(rows, schema=["Portfolio", "Statistic", *headers], orient="row"))


def show_spreads(results, label):
    columns = [*control_ports, "Avg", "Diff"]
    rows = [
        [variable_labels[variable], statistic,
         *[format_fit(fits[5, model][column], "Intercept") for column in columns]]
        for variable, fits in results.items()
        for model, statistic in [("Excess return", "Excess return"), ("FFC", "FFC alpha")]
    ]
    show_table(pl.DataFrame(
        rows, schema=[label, "Statistic", "1", "2", "3", "Average", "3–1"], orient="row"
    ))


def show_average_portfolios(results, label):
    rows = [
        [variable_labels[variable], statistic,
         *[format_fit(fits[group, model]["Avg"], "Intercept") for group in range(1, 6)]]
        for variable, fits in results.items()
        for model, statistic in [("Excess return", "Excess return"), ("FFC", "FFC alpha")]
    ]
    show_table(pl.DataFrame(rows, schema=[label, "Statistic", "1", "2", "3", "4", "4–1"], orient="row"))
```

## Univariate Portfolio Analysis {#univariate-sorts}

### Breakpoints {#breakpoints-and-membership}

In year $t$, let $\{X_t\}$ be the available values of the sort variable and $p_k$ the probability used for breakpoint $k$.
For $n_P$ portfolios, calculate $n_P-1$ breakpoints.

$$
B_{k,t}=\operatorname{Pctl}_{p_k}(\{X_t\}).
$$ {#eq-bem5-percentile}

The beta sort uses the 10th, 20th, 40th, 60th, 80th, and 90th percentiles.
The first and last groups each hold about a tenth of the stocks, giving a closer look at both tails of the distribution.
We use linear interpolation for the percentiles.

```{python}
def breakpoints(stocks, variable, probabilities, by):
    return stocks.group_by(by).agg(
        pl.col(variable).quantile(p, interpolation="linear").alias(f"{p:.0%}")
        for p in probabilities
    )

seven_way = [.10, .20, .40, .60, .80, .90]
beta_stocks = annual_panel.filter(pl.col("Beta").is_finite())
beta_breaks = breakpoints(beta_stocks, "Beta", seven_way, ["year"])
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-breakpoints
#| tbl-cap: Annual breakpoints for beta portfolios (BEM Table 5.1)
#| echo: false

show_table(beta_breaks.sort("year").rename({"year": "Year"}))
```

### Portfolio Formation

With $B_{0,t}=-\infty$ and $B_{n_P,t}=\infty$, portfolio $k$ contains

$$
P_{k,t}=\{i:B_{k-1,t}\le X_{i,t}\le B_{k,t}\}.
$$ {#eq-bem5-membership}

Both endpoints are included, as in BEM.
A stock exactly on a breakpoint can enter both adjacent portfolios.
The code joins each stock to its year's breakpoint intervals, then keeps the intervals that contain its sort value.

```{python}
from itertools import pairwise

def form_portfolios(stocks, variable, breaks, by, label):
    cutoffs = [pl.col(column) for column in breaks.columns if column not in by]
    edges = [pl.lit(-float("inf")), *cutoffs, pl.lit(float("inf"))]
    intervals = pl.concat([
        breaks.select(*by, pl.lit(group).alias(label), lower=lower, upper=upper)
        for group, (lower, upper) in enumerate(pairwise(edges), 1)
    ])
    return (
        stocks.join(intervals, on=by)
        .filter(pl.col(variable).is_between("lower", "upper"))
        .drop("lower", "upper")
    )

beta_members = form_portfolios(beta_stocks, "Beta", beta_breaks, ["year"], "portfolio")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-counts
#| tbl-cap: Annual stock counts for beta portfolios (BEM Table 5.2)
#| echo: false

show_table(
    beta_members.group_by("year", "portfolio").len()
    .pivot(on="portfolio", index="year", values="len", sort_columns=True)
    .sort("year").rename({"year": "Year"})
)
```

### Average Portfolio Values {#holding-period-returns}

For an available outcome $Y$ and weight $W$, the portfolio outcome is

$$
Y_{k,t}=\frac{\sum_{i\in P_{k,t}} W_{i,t}Y_{i,t}}
              {\sum_{i\in P_{k,t}} W_{i,t}}.
$$ {#eq-bem5-weighted}

Here $Y_{i,t}$ is the stock's excess return in year $t+1$.
For equal weights use $W_{i,t}=1$.
For value weights use December market capitalization and calculate the numerator and denominator on the same set of stocks with available returns and weights.
For each year, form the high-minus-low spread

$$
Y_{\mathrm{Diff},t}=Y_{n_P,t}-Y_{1,t}.
$$ {#eq-bem5-spread}

```{python}
portfolio_columns = [str(group) for group in range(1, 8)]
univariate_columns = [*portfolio_columns, "7–1"]
last_holding_year = 2012

def univariate_series(cells, outcome):
    return (
        cells.pivot(on="portfolio", index="year", values=outcome)
        .sort("year")
        .select("year", *portfolio_columns, (pl.col("7") - pl.col("1")).alias("7–1"))
    )

r = pl.col("excess")
valid = pl.all_horizontal(r.is_finite(), pl.col("MktCap").is_finite())
w = pl.col("MktCap").filter(valid)
beta_returns = (
    beta_members.filter(pl.col("year") < last_holding_year)
    .group_by("year", "portfolio")
    .agg(EW=r.mean(), VW=(w * r.filter(valid)).sum() / w.sum())
    .with_columns(pl.col("VW").fill_nan(None))
)
beta_ew = univariate_series(beta_returns, "EW")
beta_vw = univariate_series(beta_returns, "VW")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-equal
#| tbl-cap: Equal-weighted beta portfolio excess returns in percent (BEM Table 5.3)
#| echo: false

show_holding_year(beta_ew)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-value
#| tbl-cap: Value-weighted beta portfolio excess returns in percent (BEM Table 5.4)
#| echo: false

show_holding_year(beta_vw)
```

The 2012 formation cohort appears in the membership tables.
The last holding year in the return tables is 2012.

### Summarizing the Results {#time-series-averages-and-inference}

Average the portfolio outcomes and the spreads across the $T$ available holding years.

$$
\bar{Y}_k=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T Y_{k,t}.
$$ {#eq-bem5-average}

$$
\bar{Y}_{\mathrm{Diff}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T Y_{\mathrm{Diff},t}.
$$ {#eq-bem5-average-spread}

An intercept-only regression gives the same time-series mean.
We use StatsPAI and six Newey–West lags for inference, as specified by BEM.

```{python}
beta_means = fit_portfolios(beta_ew, univariate_columns)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-inference
#| tbl-cap: Equal-weighted beta portfolio means and inference (BEM Table 5.5)
#| echo: false

rows = {"Statistic": ["Average", "Standard error", "t-statistic", "p-value"]}
for column, fit in beta_means.items():
    rows[column] = [
        fit.params["Intercept"], fit.std_errors["Intercept"],
        fit.tvalues["Intercept"], fit.pvalues["Intercept"],
    ]
show_table(pl.DataFrame(rows))
```

### Interpreting the Results

In @tbl-bem5-sorts, the high-minus-low spread is negative for beta and market capitalization and positive for book-to-market.

```{python}
show_table(pl.DataFrame({
```

[]{#sort-on-size-or-book-to-market}

The same percentile cutoffs can be applied to other sort variables.
Recompute the breakpoints with the available observations for each variable.
Use the signed book-to-market ratio from @sec-summary-characteristics.

```{python}
def univariate_sort(variable):
    stocks = annual_panel.filter(pl.col(variable).is_finite())
    breaks = breakpoints(stocks, variable, seven_way, ["year"])
    return form_portfolios(stocks, variable, breaks, ["year"], "portfolio")

univariate_means = {"Beta": beta_means}
for variable in ["MktCap", "BM"]:
    members = univariate_sort(variable)
    returns = (
        members.filter(pl.col("year") < last_holding_year)
        .group_by("year", "portfolio").agg(pl.col("excess").mean())
    )
    series = univariate_series(returns, "excess")
    univariate_means[variable] = fit_portfolios(series, univariate_columns)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-sorts
#| tbl-cap: Equal-weighted excess returns by sort variable (BEM Table 5.8)
#| echo: false

show_table(pl.DataFrame(
    [[variable_labels[variable], *[format_fit(fit, "Intercept") for fit in fits.values()]]
     for variable, fits in univariate_means.items()],
    schema=["Sort variable", *univariate_columns], orient="row",
))
```

### Analyzing Returns {#risk-adjusted-returns}

Regress each annual portfolio return on factors from the same **holding year**.
We use the published annual series from the Kenneth French Data Library, taking the [three factors from the July 2016 archive](https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/Data_Library/f-f_factors_archive.html) and [momentum from the December 2024 legacy archive](https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/data_library_202412_archive.html).
The factors and portfolio outcomes are in percent.

The market model, Fama–French three-factor model, and Carhart four-factor model are

$$
r_{p,t}=\alpha+\beta_{\mathrm{MKT}}\mathrm{MKT}_t+\epsilon_t,
$$ {#eq-bem5-capm}

$$
r_{p,t}=\alpha+\beta_{\mathrm{MKT}}\mathrm{MKT}_t+
\beta_{\mathrm{SMB}}\mathrm{SMB}_t+\beta_{\mathrm{HML}}\mathrm{HML}_t+\epsilon_t,
$$ {#eq-bem5-ff}

$$
r_{p,t}=\alpha+\beta_{\mathrm{MKT}}\mathrm{MKT}_t+
\beta_{\mathrm{SMB}}\mathrm{SMB}_t+\beta_{\mathrm{HML}}\mathrm{HML}_t+
\beta_{\mathrm{MOM}}\mathrm{MOM}_t+\epsilon_t.
$$ {#eq-bem5-ffc}

The intercept is the portfolio's alpha under the chosen model.
For a zero-cost spread, the outcome is the difference between the two legs' excess returns.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-risk-adjusted
#| tbl-cap: Beta portfolio alphas and factor loadings (BEM Table 5.9)
#| echo: false

rows = []
for model, terms in factor_models.items():
    fits = beta_means if model == "Excess return" else fit_portfolios(beta_ew, univariate_columns, model)
    intercept_label = "Mean" if model == "Excess return" else "Alpha"
    for term in ["Intercept", *terms]:
        label = intercept_label if term == "Intercept" else f"`{term.lower()}`"
        rows.append([model, label, *[format_fit(fit, term) for fit in fits.values()]])
show_table(pl.DataFrame(rows, schema=["Model", "Coefficient", *univariate_columns], orient="row"))
```

## Bivariate Independent-Sort Analysis {#bivariate-independent-sorts}

### Breakpoints {#two-sets-of-breakpoints}

To study returns across market-cap groups while controlling for beta, keep stocks with both characteristics.
For an independent sort, calculate both sets of breakpoints across this same cross-section.
Let $j$ index the $n_1$ groups of $X_1$ and $k$ index the $n_2$ groups of $X_2$.

$$
B_{1j,t}=\operatorname{Pctl}_{p_{1j}}(\{X_{1t}\}).
$$ {#eq-bem5-first-breaks}

$$
B_{2k,t}=\operatorname{Pctl}_{p_{2k}}(\{X_{2t}\}).
$$ {#eq-bem5-second-breaks}

We use the 30th and 70th percentiles for beta and the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles for market capitalization.

Use the same percentile and membership functions as in the univariate sort.
The second set of breakpoints is grouped only by year here.
The dependent sort uses the same pipeline with an additional grouping key for the first portfolio.

```{python}
control_ports = ["1", "2", "3"]

def bivariate_sort(first, second, *, dependent=False):
    stocks = annual_panel.filter(pl.all_horizontal(pl.col(first, second).is_finite()))
    first_breaks = breakpoints(stocks, first, [.30, .70], ["year"])
    first_groups = form_portfolios(stocks, first, first_breaks, ["year"], "control")

    by = ["year", "control"] if dependent else ["year"]
    breakpoint_sample = first_groups if dependent else stocks
    second_breaks = breakpoints(breakpoint_sample, second, [.25, .50, .75], by)
    members = form_portfolios(first_groups, second, second_breaks, by, "target")
    return members, first_breaks, second_breaks

independent, first_breaks, second_breaks = bivariate_sort("Beta", "MktCap")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-independent-breaks
#| tbl-cap: Annual breakpoints for the independent beta and market-cap sorts (BEM Table 5.10)
#| echo: false

show_table(first_breaks.join(second_breaks, on="year", validate="1:1").sort("year").rename({
    "year": "Year", "30%": "Beta 30%", "70%": "Beta 70%", "25%": "Market cap 25%",
    "50%": "Market cap 50%", "75%": "Market cap 75%",
}))
```

### Portfolio Formation

A portfolio is the intersection of a beta group and a market-cap group.

$$
P_{j,k,t}=
\{i:B_{1,j-1,t}\le X_{1i,t}\le B_{1j,t}\}
\cap
\{i:B_{2,k-1,t}\le X_{2i,t}\le B_{2k,t}\}.
$$ {#eq-bem5-independent-membership}

Pivot the portfolio cells so that the beta groups are columns and the market-cap groups are rows within each year.

```{python}
def control_grid(cells, value):
    return (
        cells.pivot(on="control", index=["year", "target"], values=value)
        .sort("year", "target")
        .select("year", "target", *control_ports)
    )
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-independent-counts
#| tbl-cap: Annual counts in the independent beta and market-cap portfolios (BEM Table 5.11)
#| echo: false

independent_counts = independent.group_by("year", "control", "target").len()
show_grid(control_grid(independent_counts, "len"), "Beta", "MktCap")
```

### Average Portfolio Values {#returns-spreads-and-average-portfolios}

Within each of the 12 portfolios, compute the outcome using the univariate weighting rule.
The example uses equal weights.

$$
Y_{j,k,t}=\frac{\sum_{i\in P_{j,k,t}}W_{i,t}Y_{i,t}}
                {\sum_{i\in P_{j,k,t}}W_{i,t}}.
$$ {#eq-bem5-grid-outcome}

A high-minus-low spread along market capitalization holds the beta group fixed.
A spread along beta holds the market-cap group fixed.

$$
Y_{j,\mathrm{Diff},t}=Y_{j,n_2,t}-Y_{j,1,t}.
$$ {#eq-bem5-target-spread}

$$
Y_{\mathrm{Diff},k,t}=Y_{n_1,k,t}-Y_{1,k,t}.
$$ {#eq-bem5-control-spread}

We can also average across either set of portfolios.
Each group receives equal weight, even when stock counts differ.

$$
Y_{\mathrm{Avg},k,t}=\frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_1}Y_{j,k,t}.
$$ {#eq-bem5-control-average}

$$
Y_{j,\mathrm{Avg},t}=\frac{1}{n_2}\sum_{k=1}^{n_2}Y_{j,k,t}.
$$ {#eq-bem5-target-average}

$$
Y_{\mathrm{Avg},\mathrm{Avg},t}
=\frac{1}{n_1}\sum_jY_{j,\mathrm{Avg},t}
=\frac{1}{n_2}\sum_kY_{\mathrm{Avg},k,t}
=\frac{1}{n_1n_2}\sum_j\sum_kY_{j,k,t}.
$$ {#eq-bem5-grand-average}

The difference in differences compares the market-cap spread in the highest-beta group with the spread in the lowest-beta group.
The same result comes from comparing beta spreads across market-cap groups.

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_{\mathrm{Diff},\mathrm{Diff},t}
 &=Y_{n_1,n_2,t}-Y_{n_1,1,t}-Y_{1,n_2,t}+Y_{1,1,t}\\
 &=Y_{\mathrm{Diff},n_2,t}-Y_{\mathrm{Diff},1,t}\\
 &=Y_{n_1,\mathrm{Diff},t}-Y_{1,\mathrm{Diff},t}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-bem5-difference-in-differences}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-spread-diagram
#| tbl-cap: Constructing the difference in differences from the four corner portfolios (BEM Table 5.12)
#| echo: false

show_table(pl.DataFrame({
    "Second sort": ["Low", "High", "High minus low"],
    "First sort low": ["$A$", "$C$", "$C-A$"],
    "First sort high": ["$B$", "$D$", "$D-B$"],
    "First sort high minus low": ["$B-A$", "$D-C$", "$(D-C)-(B-A)=(D-B)-(C-A)$"],
}))
```

Compute the spreads and averages within each holding year before fitting their time-series means or alphas.
This preserves the covariance between the portfolio legs in the reported standard errors.

```{python}
def bivariate_returns(members, *, dependent=False):
    cells = (
        members.filter(pl.col("year") < last_holding_year)
        .group_by("year", "control", "target").agg(pl.col("excess").mean())
    )
    grid = control_grid(cells, "excess")
    control_returns = pl.col(control_ports)
    spread = grid.group_by("year").agg(
        control_returns.filter(pl.col("target") == 4).first()
        - control_returns.filter(pl.col("target") == 1).first()
    ).with_columns(target=pl.lit(5))

    rows = [grid, spread.select(grid.columns)]
    if not dependent:
        average = grid.group_by("year").agg(pl.col(control_ports).mean()).with_columns(target=pl.lit(6))
        rows.append(average.select(grid.columns))
    return (
        pl.concat(rows).sort("year", "target")
        .with_columns(Diff=pl.col("3") - pl.col("1"),
                      Avg=pl.mean_horizontal(control_ports, ignore_nulls=False))
    )

independent_returns = bivariate_returns(independent)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-independent-returns
#| tbl-cap: Annual equal-weighted returns for the independent sorts (BEM Table 5.13)
#| echo: false

show_grid(independent_returns, "Beta", "MktCap", holding=True)
```

### Summarizing the Results {#summarize-and-present-the-returns}

The full return grid reports both excess returns and four-factor alphas.
The next tables show ways to focus on a specific spread or on the return profile after averaging across the control groups.

```{python}
independent_fits = grid_fits(independent_returns)
```

```{python}
#| tbl-cap: Excess returns and four-factor alphas for the independent sorts (BEM Table 5.14)

show_grid_fits(independent_fits)
```

### Interpreting the Results

### Presenting the Results

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-independent-alphas
#| tbl-cap: Compact four-factor alpha grid for the independent sorts (BEM Table 5.15)
#| echo: false

rows = []
for group in range(1, 7):
    fits = independent_fits[group, "FFC"]
    row = [
        format_fit(fits[c], "Intercept") if c in ["Diff", "Avg"] or group > 4
        else f"{fits[c].params['Intercept']:.2f}"
        for c in [*control_ports, "Diff", "Avg"]
    ]
    if group == 6:
        row[-1] = None
    rows.append([target_label("MktCap", group), *row])
show_table(pl.DataFrame(rows, schema=["Portfolio", "Beta 1", "Beta 2", "Beta 3", "Beta 3–1",
                                     "Beta average"], orient="row"))
```

To check the size effect with a different control, group on book-to-market first and market capitalization second.
Both sets of breakpoints still use the entire cross-section of eligible stocks.

## Bivariate Dependent-Sort Analysis {#bivariate-dependent-sorts}

### Breakpoints {#breakpoints-within-control-groups}

Start with the same beta groups.
For each year and each beta group, calculate the market-cap quartiles within the group.
If $P^{(1)}_{j,t}$ is the set of stocks in beta group $j$, its market-cap breakpoint $k$ is

$$
B_{2j,k,t}=\operatorname{Pctl}_{p_{2k}}(\{X_{2i,t}:i\in P^{(1)}_{j,t}\}).
$$ {#eq-bem5-conditional-breaks}

```{python}
dependent, beta_cutoffs, conditional_cutoffs = bivariate_sort("Beta", "MktCap", dependent=True)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-dependent-breaks
#| tbl-cap: Annual market-cap breakpoints within each beta group (BEM Table 5.20)
#| echo: false

show_table(
    conditional_cutoffs.join(beta_cutoffs, on="year", validate="m:1")
    .sort("year", "control")
    .select("year", "control", "30%", "70%", "25%", "50%", "75%")
    .rename({"year": "Year", "control": "Beta group", "30%": "Beta 30%", "70%": "Beta 70%",
             "25%": "Market cap 25%", "50%": "Market cap 50%", "75%": "Market cap 75%"})
)
```

### Portfolio Formation

The portfolios now use those group-specific market-cap breakpoints.

$$
P_{j,k,t}=
\{i:B_{1,j-1,t}\le X_{1i,t}\le B_{1j,t}\}
\cap
\{i:B_{2j,k-1,t}\le X_{2i,t}\le B_{2j,k,t}\}.
$$ {#eq-bem5-dependent-membership}

BEM's printed equation (5.21) leaves the upper endpoint open.
The discussion of Table 5.21 assigns a stock on a breakpoint to both adjacent portfolios, so we use inclusive endpoints here as well.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-dependent-counts
#| tbl-cap: Annual counts in the dependent beta and market-cap portfolios (BEM Table 5.21)
#| echo: false

dependent_counts = dependent.group_by("year", "control", "target").len()
show_grid(control_grid(dependent_counts, "len"), "Beta", "MktCap")
```

Conditional quartiles tend to distribute stocks evenly within each beta group.
In the independent sort, the largest stocks are much more common in the high-beta group than in the low-beta group.
@fig-bem5-counts compares average stock counts across the two sorts.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bem5-counts
#| fig-cap: Average annual stock counts by beta group and market-cap quartile
#| fig-alt: Heatmaps show uneven counts across cells under independent sorting and approximately equal counts down each beta-group column under dependent sorting.
#| echo: false

sort_methods = ["Independent", "Dependent"]
average_counts = pl.concat(
    counts.group_by("control", "target").agg(count=pl.col("len").mean())
    .with_columns(method=pl.lit(method, dtype=pl.Enum(sort_methods)))
    for method, counts in zip(sort_methods, [independent_counts, dependent_counts], strict=True)
)
max_count = average_counts["count"].max()
(
    average_counts.with_columns(
        label=pl.col("count").round().cast(pl.Int64),
        label_color=pl.when(pl.col("count") > 0.58 * max_count)
        .then(pl.lit("white")).otherwise(pl.lit("#172b4d")),
    )
    .ggplot(aes(x="control", y="target", fill="count"))
    .geom_tile()
    .geom_text(aes(label="label", color="label_color"))
    .facet_wrap("method", nrow=1)
    .scale_fill_gradient(low="#f7fbff", high="#08306b", limits=(0, max_count), guide=None)
    .scale_color_identity()
    .scale_x_continuous(breaks=range(1, 4), expand=(0, 0))
    .scale_y_reverse(breaks=range(1, 5), expand=(0, 0))
    .labs(x="Beta group", y="Market-cap quartile")
    .theme_minimal()
    .add_theme(figure_size=(8, 4), panel_grid=element_blank())
)
```

### Average Portfolio Values {#returns-and-inference}

Calculate returns and high-minus-low spreads within each beta group, then average the three groups.

```{python}
dependent_returns = bivariate_returns(dependent, dependent=True)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-dependent-returns
#| tbl-cap: Annual equal-weighted returns for the dependent sorts (BEM Table 5.22)
#| echo: false

show_grid(dependent_returns.drop("Diff"), "Beta", "MktCap", holding=True)
```

### Summarizing the Results

```{python}
dependent_fits = grid_fits(dependent_returns)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-dependent-summary
#| tbl-cap: Excess returns and four-factor alphas for the dependent sorts (BEM Table 5.23)
#| echo: false

show_grid_fits(dependent_fits, dependent=True)
```

### Interpreting the Results

The high-minus-low differences across beta groups in the spread tables compare *market-cap spreads*.
They show whether the size effect varies with beta.

### Presenting the Results

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-dependent-compact
#| tbl-cap: Compact return grid and four-factor size spreads for the dependent sorts (BEM Table 5.24)
#| echo: false

columns = [*control_ports, "Avg"]
rows = [
    [target_label("MktCap", group), *[
        f"{dependent_fits[group, 'Excess return'][column].params['Intercept']:.2f}"
        for column in columns
    ]]
    for group in range(1, 5)
]
rows += [
    [label, *[format_fit(dependent_fits[5, model][column], "Intercept") for column in columns]]
    for label, model in [("Market cap 4–1", "Excess return"), ("FFC alpha", "FFC")]
]
show_table(pl.DataFrame(rows, schema=["Portfolio", "Beta 1", "Beta 2", "Beta 3", "Beta average"],
                        orient="row"))
```

The same dependent sort can use book-to-market as the first variable or the second variable.
The following tables keep the sort order explicit.

```{python}
dependent_beta_bm, _, _ = bivariate_sort("Beta", "BM", dependent=True)

dependent_cap_controls = {
    "Beta": dependent_fits,
    "BM": grid_fits(bivariate_returns(dependent_bm_cap, dependent=True)),
}
dependent_beta_controls = {
    "MktCap": dependent_fits,
    "BM": grid_fits(bivariate_returns(dependent_beta_bm, dependent=True)),
}
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-dependent-size-spreads
#| tbl-cap: Dependent-sort size spreads by control variable (BEM Table 5.25)
#| echo: false

show_spreads(dependent_cap_controls, "Control")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-dependent-size-averages
#| tbl-cap: Dependent-sort size portfolios averaged across control groups (BEM Table 5.26)
#| echo: false

show_average_portfolios(dependent_cap_controls, "Control")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-dependent-target-spreads
#| tbl-cap: Dependent-sort size and book-to-market spreads by beta group (BEM Table 5.27)
#| echo: false

show_spreads(dependent_beta_controls, "Sort variable")
```

In @tbl-bem5-dependent-target-spreads, the four-factor alpha of the book-to-market spread is smaller in the highest-beta group than in the lowest-beta group.[^dependent-bm-alpha]

[^dependent-bm-alpha]: The difference is statistically significant here ($t=-3.55$). BEM Table 5.27 reports $t=-1.46$ for the same comparison.

```{python}

#| tbl-cap: Dependent-sort size and book-to-market portfolios averaged across beta groups (BEM Table 5.28)
#| echo: false

```

## Independent Versus Dependent Sort {#compare-the-two-sorts}

Average market capitalization makes the difference between the two methods concrete.
An independent sort applies the same market-cap cutoffs across beta groups.
A dependent sort can classify a stock as large among low-beta stocks even if its capitalization would place it in a lower quartile among high-beta stocks.

```{python}
def average_capitalization(members):
    return (
        members.group_by("year", "control", "target").agg(pl.col("MktCap").mean())
        .group_by("control", "target").agg(pl.col("MktCap").mean())
        .pivot(on="control", index="target", values="MktCap")
        .sort("target").select("target", *control_ports)
    )

independent_caps = average_capitalization(independent)
dependent_caps = average_capitalization(dependent)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-independent-capitalization
#| tbl-cap: Average market capitalization in the independent sorts, millions of dollars (BEM Table 5.29)
#| echo: false

show_grid(independent_caps.with_columns(pl.col(control_ports).round().cast(pl.Int64)), "Beta", "MktCap")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem5-dependent-capitalization
#| tbl-cap: Average market capitalization in the dependent sorts, millions of dollars (BEM Table 5.30)
#| echo: false

show_grid(dependent_caps.with_columns(pl.col(control_ports).round().cast(pl.Int64)), "Beta", "MktCap")
```

@fig-bem5-capitalization plots the same means on a log scale.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bem5-capitalization
#| fig-cap: Market-cap profiles in independent and dependent sorts
#| fig-alt: Within market-cap quartiles, average market caps are similar across beta groups in the independent sort. The dependent sort shows much wider differences across beta groups.
#| echo: false

capitalization = pl.concat(
    caps.unpivot(index="target", variable_name="group", value_name="cap")
    .with_columns(method=pl.lit(method, dtype=pl.Enum(sort_methods)))
    for method, caps in zip(sort_methods, [independent_caps, dependent_caps], strict=True)
)
(
    capitalization.ggplot(aes(x="target", y="cap", color="group"))
    .geom_line()
    .geom_point(aes(shape="group"))
    .facet_wrap("method", nrow=1)
    .scale_x_continuous(breaks=range(1, 5))
    .scale_y_log10(labels=lambda values: [f"{value:,.0f}" for value in values])
    .scale_color_brewer(type="qual", palette="Dark2")
    .scale_shape_manual(values=["o", "s", "^"])
    .labs(x="Market-cap quartile", y="Average market cap ($ millions, log scale)",
          color="Beta group", shape="Beta group")
    .theme_minimal()
    .add_theme(figure_size=(8, 3.7), legend_position="top")
)
```

## Trivariate-Sort Analysis

A third sort variable can be added by forming another unconditional group or by calculating its breakpoints within the existing intersected groups.
With three variables the number of portfolios grows quickly, so check the stock counts before interpreting portfolio spreads.
